1.pericope_label: And it came to pass, that, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said unto him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin both address the relation to Matthew’s account. Gill holds that these directions, though agreeing in substance with the earlier ones, were delivered at another time, in another place and on another occasion: Christ was then in Galilee and is here in Judea; the earlier were given unasked and in the course of preaching, these at the request of a disciple and immediately after he had been praying. He adds that the one who spoke did so in the name of the rest. Calvin leaves the question open, observing that some think the form was delivered twice because Luke reports a request where Matthew has Christ teach it of his own accord, but recalling that Matthew collects the leading points of the teaching rather than always preserving the occasion.

Henry begins from prayer as one of the great laws of natural religion — the man who never prays, never gives glory to his Maker and never owns his dependence is a monster — and makes it one great design of Christianity to assist us in it. He notes that Luke records Christ praying more often than any other evangelist, that as God he was prayed to and as man he prayed, and that though he was a Son he learned obedience. He draws two practical points from the disciples’ approach: the gifts and graces of others should make us covet the same and provoke a holy emulation, and they waited until he had ceased rather than interrupt him even with so good a motion, since everything is beautiful in its season.

Lightfoot, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all treat the request as a historical puzzle. Lightfoot asks how the disciple could want a form when the Sermon on the Mount had already given one, and concludes he was asking for a rule of prayer answering to what John had given his followers — a badge of discipleship rather than a remedy for ignorance. Barnes catalogues Luke’s notices of Christ at prayer (the baptism, the wilderness, the night before the apostles were chosen, the solitary prayer, the transfiguration) and supposes the disciples were struck by the excellence and fervour of what they heard. Ellicott argues from Jewish practice and from the parallels that our Lord prayed aloud and that some at least of the disciples overheard him, listening without being able to follow or record, and wanting to enter into his spirit. Robertson notes the characteristically Lukan construction of the opening clause and that Jesus had already taught this by precept and example, so that the occasion revived rather than began their interest.

Wesley explains the request from a known custom rather than from any defect in the disciples: the Jewish masters used to give their followers a short form of prayer as a peculiar badge of their relation to them, and John the Baptist had probably done the same. On that reading the disciples are asking for the mark of their discipleship, and Christ answers by repeating the form already given in the Sermon on the Mount and enlarging on it, still speaking the same things in substance.

Titus, Gregory of Nyssa and Basil each contribute a short link to the chain. Titus explains the request from what the disciples had just seen: a new way of life calls for a new form of prayer, and they wished not to sin against God by asking for one thing instead of another, or by approaching him in a manner they ought not, the Old Testament prayers being already many. Gregory of Nyssa notes only that Christ unfolds the teaching of prayer to disciples who wisely desired that knowledge. Basil divides prayer into two kinds, one composed of praise with humiliation and one of petition; he warns against opening with petition rather than with the praise of him who created all things, and, on the last clause, holds that we should not ask for bodily afflictions but, once already in temptation, should ask for the power to endure.

Origen and Cyril both move quickly from the request to the petitions. Origen notes that the disciple appeals to John as the pattern, and then presses the first petition: the name of God is given by idolaters and by those in error to idols and creatures, and so has not yet been made holy in the sense of being set apart. Cyril takes up the daily bread and defends its plain sense against those who think it unfitting for saints to seek bodily goods from God and therefore read the words spiritually. The chief concern of the saints should indeed be spiritual gifts, but they may seek their common bread without blame; and since it is not the part of those who have bread to ask for it, the very command implies that they should possess nothing and practise an honourable poverty.

Bede, Pseudo-Augustine, Augustine and Tertullian occupy very different ground. Bede reads the verse against the two sisters of the previous chapter, who signified the two lives of the Church, and finds that the prayer Christ taught contains the mystery of each, the perfection of those lives being obtained by prayer and not by our own strength. Pseudo-Augustine expounds the first petition as a prayer for the cleansing of the whole world, that God’s holiness be known to all and worthily praised. Augustine reconciles the evangelists: Matthew seems to have seven petitions and Luke five, but Luke’s brevity shows how the seven are to be taken, the third being in a manner a repetition of the two before it and therefore omitted. Tertullian is not expounding but disputing — he takes the disciple’s request as proof that his opponent’s scheme requires different prayers for different gods, the Father addressed here being on that scheme not the Creator.

debates: Whether this is the same occasion as the Sermon on the Mount. Gill argues for two distinct deliveries from the change of place, of audience and of prompting; Wesley treats it as a repetition with enlargement; Calvin declines to settle it, noting only that Matthew arranges by topic. Lightfoot raises the sharper form of the problem — why ask for a form you have already been given — and answers that what was wanted was a badge like John’s.

How the two versions of the prayer relate. Augustine holds that Matthew’s seven petitions and Luke’s five do not disagree, Luke having compressed by treating one petition as a repetition of the two preceding.

Whether the daily bread may be understood of ordinary food. Cyril records that some think it unfit for saints to seek bodily goods and so assign the words a spiritual sense; he allows the spiritual priority but defends the literal request, and turns it into an argument for poverty.
outliers: Tertullian alone is not interpreting the verse but using it as evidence in a dispute, reading the disciple’s request as an admission that different gods would need different prayers; the tone is polemical where every other witness here is expository.
Henry alone draws a rule of manners from the timing — that the disciples waited until Christ had ceased before speaking, since even a good motion may be brought at the wrong moment.
themes: John’s form and the badge of discipleship
relation to the Sermon on the Mount
prayer and the two lives of the Church

2.pericope_label: And he said unto them, When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth. Give us day by day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil.

schools.summary: Gill attends to the address and to the text. He observes that although a single disciple had made the request, Christ directed his answer to them all, both because the one spoke in the name of the rest and because the instruction concerned every one of them, including those who had heard the earlier form and those who had not. On the third petition he records that the words may be rendered day by day, or for the day, or with the Syriac every day; and on the fourth that Beza’s most ancient copy reads debts where the common text has sins, a reading which agrees best with the indebted of the clause that follows.

Ellicott, Barnes and Lightfoot divide the work between form, doctrine and background. Ellicott treats the near-identity with the Sermon on the Mount as significant rather than awkward, allowing that the small verbal differences may be the reporter’s; what had sufficed for the multitude sufficed here, and for anyone whose desires did not spontaneously find words this shortest of prayers contained all he should ask. Barnes notes that Luke’s form of the clause on forgiving differs from Matthew’s while the sense is one, and is careful about what it claims: unless we come forgiving all others we cannot expect pardon, but forgiveness is not thereby deserved or merited — it is a state of mind without which God cannot consistently pardon, and those indebted are those who have injured us. Lightfoot reads the petition against temptation as directed principally against the visible apparitions of the devil and his actual obsessions, which he thinks much softens the difficulty of God ‘leading’ anyone into temptation, and accounts for the absent doxology by the purpose of the moment, which was to deliver a form merely petitionary.

Wesley and Clarke both press the prayer toward use. Wesley holds that what Christ said to the disciples is undoubtedly said to us also, so that we are directed not merely to imitate this in our prayers but to use this very form; and on the fourth petition he insists the forgiving is continual rather than once for all, while denying that it is the meritorious cause of our pardon — it removes the hindrance that would otherwise make pardon impossible. Clarke takes over Lightfoot’s reading of the petition about temptation as aimed at the devil’s visible apparitions and obsessions, and objects to the Authorised rendering of the last clause: deliver us from evil is a very inadequate translation, and the sense is deliver us from the wicked one.

Cyril of Jerusalem approaches the prayer as liturgy. He describes the congregation coming, after all that has gone before, to say the prayer the Saviour delivered to his disciples, entitling God Father with a pure conscience; and he makes the address itself the marvel, since God has given those who revolted from him and were in the extreme of misery so complete a forgiveness and so great a participation of grace that they may call him Father. On the final petition he presses the objection that scripture elsewhere calls the untempted man unproved and bids us count it joy to fall into divers temptations, and resolves it by distinguishing being tempted from entering into temptation: temptation is a winter torrent difficult to cross, and those who are not overwhelmed pass through it.

Cyril of Alexandria expounds the prayer as a spiritual feast. Where the rich invite the friends they wish to honour and set out a costly banquet that satisfies nothing but appetite, the Saviour feasts the hearts of those who would live virtuously with the saving doctrine of the gospel, by which a man becomes full of good and an heir of eternal life. He praises the insatiate desire of learning, citing the beatitude on those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, and holds that understanding these words correctly requires divine light — hence David’s prayer to be led into God’s truth and taught. On the daily bread he records the objection that it is unsuitable for saints to ask God for corporeal things, and the consequent move to a purely spiritual reading; he grants that spiritual gifts should be their chief endeavour but refuses the diversion, holding that they may ask for simple bread at the Saviour’s own command with an address to God free from all blame.

debates: Whether the last petition asks to escape temptation altogether. Cyril of Jerusalem denies it, since scripture calls the untempted man unproved, and distinguishes being tempted from being overwhelmed. Lightfoot and Clarke narrow the petition instead to the devil’s visible apparitions and obsessions, which they think removes the difficulty about God leading anyone into temptation.

Whether the daily bread is bodily or spiritual. Cyril of Alexandria reports that some think it unfitting for saints to ask God for corporeal things and so read the petition spiritually; he allows the priority of spiritual gifts but defends the literal request as blameless.

What the clause on forgiving asserts. Barnes and Wesley agree that it states a condition and not a merit — Barnes calling it a disposition without which God cannot consistently pardon, Wesley the removal of a hindrance rather than a meritorious cause — and Wesley adds that the forgiving must be continual.
Why the doxology is absent. Lightfoot explains it from the occasion, Christ intending here to give a form merely petitionary.
outliers: Cyril of Jerusalem is describing what a congregation does rather than what a text means: his account is of the prayer’s place in worship, spoken after other things and with a pure conscience, where every other witness here is expounding the words.
Gill is alone in citing a manuscript reading, Beza’s copy with debts for sins, and in preferring it on the internal ground that it matches the indebted of the next clause.
themes: the kingdom and the will of God
deliver us from the wicked one
relation to the Sermon on the Mount

5.pericope_label: And he said unto them, Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say unto him, Friend, lend me three loaves; For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him? And he from within shall answer and say, Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee. I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin keep to the plain sense. Gill glosses the friend as a neighbour or acquaintance, presses the traveller’s condition — out of the way, having lost his road, benighted, and arriving after wandering some time — and records that the Vulgate premises to the last verse the words ‘if he continue knocking’. Calvin notes that the comparison is absent from Matthew and draws the general instruction: believers ought not to be discouraged if they do not immediately obtain their desires, or find them difficult to obtain; if importunity of asking among men extorts what a person would not willingly do, there is no reason to doubt that God will listen to those who persevere constantly in prayer and whose minds do not slacken through difficulty or delay.

Henry treats the passage as encouragement to fervency and constancy. We must come for what we need as a man comes to a neighbour who is kind to him, and we must come for bread — that is, for what is needful; if God does not answer our prayers speedily he will answer in due time, provided we continue to pray.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the story as an illustration with a single point. Barnes holds the design is solely to show the necessity of being importunate, explains midnight as the hour when help is most inconvenient, and defines importunity as troublesome perseverance that refuses to take a denial — an improper perseverance, effective only because the sleeper preferred to rise rather than be further disturbed; he judges the Vulgate’s added clause about continued knocking indispensable to the sense though absent from the Greek. Ellicott declines to call the passage a parable, notes that it is peculiar to Luke and characteristic of him, and admires the familiar tone and dramatic vividness as almost unique; midnight is chosen as the hour men most expect to be left to their repose, the three loaves are one each for host, guest and reserve, and the scene is a poor man’s single room. He warns expressly that the illustrative matter cannot be pressed into an interpretation and yields only an argument a fortiori — thus man might answer, but so does not God — and glosses the key word as literally shamelessness, found nowhere else in the New Testament. Robertson confirms both rarities, adding that the verb for lending is the friendly loan and not the loan at interest, rendering the refusal ‘stop furnishing troubles to me’, and observing that the shut door stands in the perfect tense, shut to stay shut.

Wesley and Clarke both work on the detail of the scene. Wesley takes midnight as the most unseasonable time imaginable and turns it directly into comfort: no time is unseasonable with God, either for hearing or for answering prayer. Clarke renders the traveller’s arrival more literally — a friend is come to me out of his way, benighted, belated, having lost his road — and thinks this makes the case more urgent and the demand for prompt relief stronger; on the sleeper’s reply he prefers Bishop Pearce’s rendering, that I and my children are in bed, and he records the clause about persevering in knocking as attested by the Armenian, the Vulgate and four copies of the Itala.

Theophylact and Gregory of Nyssa contribute alternative allegories. Theophylact offers two without choosing between them: either the midnight is the end of life, at which many come to God, and the friend is the angel who receives the soul; or the midnight is the depth of temptations, in which one who has fallen seeks three loaves as relief for the wants of body, soul and spirit, and the friend arriving from his journey is God himself, who tries by temptations the man who has nothing to set before him. Gregory of Nyssa, taken up by the chain immediately after Augustine, reads the children in bed as those who by the arms of righteousness have claimed freedom from passion, and adds that the good we acquire by practice was from the beginning laid up in our nature.

Cyril supplies the motive for the parable in its context. The Saviour had taught the form of prayer in answer to the apostles’ request; the danger was that those who received it would use it carelessly and languidly, and give up when they were not heard at the first or second asking. The story is told against that danger, and its lesson is stated as a contrast: cowardice in our prayers is hurtful, patience in them of great advantage.

Gloss, Ambrose and Augustine read the scene as figure. Gloss denies that the difficulty of obtaining takes away the liberty of asking, and finds it meant rather to kindle the desire of praying. Ambrose identifies the shut door with the door Paul asked to have opened to him — seeking not only his own prayers but the people’s, that a door of utterance might be given him to speak the mystery of Christ — and suggests it may be the door John saw standing open. Augustine takes the midnight for a famine of the word, when understanding is shut up and those who dealt out the wisdom of the gospel like bread are now in their secret rest with the Lord, which is what is meant by the children being in bed with him.

debates: Whether the illustration may be allegorised at all. Ellicott says expressly that the illustrative matter cannot be pressed into an interpretation and yields only an argument from the lesser to the greater; the catena does the opposite, Augustine, Ambrose and Theophylact each assigning meanings to the midnight, the door and the loaves — and Theophylact offering two incompatible schemes in the same breath.

What the sleeper’s reluctance shows about God. Barnes has the man moved only by a wish to end the disturbance, and Calvin argues from the same reluctance a fortiori to God’s readiness; Ellicott makes the contrast explicit, that thus man might answer but so does not God.

Whether the clause about continued knocking belongs to the text. Gill reports it from the Vulgate, Clarke lists the Armenian and Italic witnesses for it, and Barnes, granting it is not in the Greek, treats it as indispensable to the sense.
outliers: Wesley alone turns the inconvenience of the hour into a positive assurance rather than an obstacle to be overcome, on the ground that no hour is unseasonable with God.

Robertson is alone in resting his reading on the tenses and the rarity of the words — the friendly-loan verb and the noun for shamelessness, each occurring only here in the New Testament, and the perfect of the shut door.
themes: an argument from lesser to greater
allegories of midnight and the loaves
perseverance when prayer is not answered at once

9.pericope_label: And I say unto you, Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone? or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent? Or if he shall ask an egg, will he offer him a scorpion? If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?

schools.summary: Gill covers both the promise and its apparent failures. He takes the exhortation as encouragement to importunity: whoever asks in the name of Christ and in faith, whether for bread for the body, food for the soul, or any blessing temporal or spiritual, receives — not according to his deserts but according to the riches of the grace of God. On the next verse he explains why some ask and do not receive: they ask amiss, applying to a wrong person, or asking in a wrong manner, from wrong principles, or with wrong ends in view; where the object, matter, manner and end are right, a man has his petitions whoever he is and however mean. On the scorpion he catalogues three kinds — land scorpions, a venomous sort of serpent; flying scorpions, reckoned a kind of fowl; and sea scorpions of the fish kind — declines to say which is meant, and notes a herb of the same name whose leaves resemble the creature.

Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott contribute the natural history and the grammar. Barnes cites Dr. Thomson’s report that there is no imaginable likeness between an egg and the ordinary black scorpion of that country in colour, size or shape, but that older writers describe a white scorpion which, with its tail folded up, would not look unlike a small egg. Robertson notes a decided anacoluthon in the construction of the question about the father, that the manuscripts differ considerably there, and that only in Luke does Jesus name the Holy Spirit as the gift; he also observes how fond Jesus is of the ‘how much more’ form of argument. Ellicott marks the same substitution as significant: the one highest gift of the Holy Spirit replaces the wider and less definite ‘good things’ of Matthew, which he takes as belonging to a later stage of the teaching and as addressed probably to some of the Seventy, who were being taught to ask boldly for the Spirit that would make them in very deed a company of prophets.

Clarke and Wesley both read the passage practically. Clarke redirects the importunity toward the one praying: be importunate with God not so much to prevail on him to save you as to bring yourself into a proper disposition to receive the mercy he is always disposed to give, since a man who is not importunate for his soul’s salvation does not feel his need of it and could not be expected to be grateful for it. On the scorpion he argues by analogy from the other pairs — eels closely resemble serpents and some stones exactly resemble bread — so that a similar resemblance between egg and scorpion is what is intended; and he records that several manuscripts read ‘the good spirit’ in the final clause. Wesley draws attention to the ascending series, a friend, a father, God, and calls the Holy Spirit the best of gifts and the one that includes every good gift.

Chrysostom, Basil and Cyril of Jerusalem each take up one strand. Chrysostom distinguishes the verbs: asking is prayer, seeking is zeal and anxiety, because what is sought requires great care — particularly so with God, since many things block up our senses; as men search for lost gold, so should we anxiously seek God. Basil states the condition on the other side: one who from indolence surrenders to his desires and betrays himself into his enemies’ hands is neither assisted nor heard, since by sin he has alienated himself from God; a man must offer what belongs to him and cry to God for help, and must ask neither slackly nor with a mind wavering to and fro, or he will provoke God to anger rather than obtain. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the last clause as a proof text on the Holy Spirit, placing it beside the words about being born of water and of the Spirit to show that this grace comes from the Father.

Cyril and Origen both press beyond the surface. Cyril takes the formula ‘I say unto you’ as carrying the force of an oath: God does not lie, and when he confirms a thing to his hearers with an oath he is exposing the inexcusable littleness of their faith. Origen raises the standing objection — how is it that people pray and are not heard? — and answers that whoever seeks in the right way, omitting nothing that avails toward obtaining, really does receive what he asked, the fault lying with those who turn away from the object of a right request. On the pairs he makes the bread the food of the soul in knowledge, without which it cannot be saved, and the fish the love of instruction, the knowledge of the world’s constitution and the effects of the elements; God gives neither the stone the devil wished Christ to eat nor a serpent in place of a fish.

Augustine and Ambrose frame the exhortation. Augustine notes that the metaphor of the previous verses is now laid aside and the command given expressly — ask, seek, knock, until we receive what we are seeking — and reads the three objects symbolically: the bread is charity, which we desire more than anything and without which all else is nothing, as a table without bread is mean; the stone set against it is hardness of heart; the fish signifies belief in things invisible. Ambrose supplies the reason a promise is attached to the command at all: one who promises anything ought to convey a hope of the thing promised, so that obedience may follow the command and faith may follow the promise.

debates: Why prayer sometimes goes unanswered. Origen locates the fault in the manner of seeking, Basil in the state of the one who asks — indolence, wavering, sin already committed — and Gill in the object, matter, manner and end of the request. None of them qualifies the promise itself.

Whether the bread, fish and egg are figures or ordinary food. Augustine and Origen read them as charity, faith in the invisible, and knowledge; Gill, Barnes and Clarke treat the question as one of natural resemblance, asking what kind of scorpion could be mistaken for an egg.

What the change from Matthew’s ‘good things’ to ‘the Holy Spirit’ means. Ellicott takes it as marking a later stage of teaching addressed to the Seventy; Robertson simply records that the substitution is peculiar to Luke; Wesley treats the Spirit as the gift that contains all the others; Clarke notes a manuscript variant reading ‘the good spirit’.
outliers: Cyril alone finds an oath in the formula ‘I say unto you’, and turns it into a rebuke of the hearers’ faith rather than a reinforcement of the promise.
Clarke alone reverses the direction of importunity, making its purpose the shaping of the one who prays rather than any effect upon God, who is described as already disposed to give.
themes: how much more your heavenly Father
the Holy Spirit as the highest gift
prayer and the disposition of the one praying

14.pericope_label: And he was casting out a devil, and it was dumb. And it came to pass, when the devil was gone out, the dumb spake; and the people wondered. But some of them said, He casteth out devils through Beelzebub the chief of the devils. And others, tempting him, sought of him a sign from heaven.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin both attend to the motives of the objectors. Gill identifies the speakers as the Pharisees, who could not bear that Christ should be thought the Messiah and therefore put an ill construction on the miracle, and takes the others who tempted him to be Scribes and Pharisees or else Sadducees. Calvin observes that Matthew and Mark record a similar demand for a sign at a later point, which shows that Christ was attacked on this subject repeatedly and that there was no end to the wickedness of men who had once resolved to oppose the truth. He reads the demand as a manoeuvre rather than an inquiry: they ask a sign so as to have a plausible pretext for unbelief, namely that Christ’s calling had not been duly attested.

Henry treats the episode as an argument rather than an incident. Christ is giving a general proof of his divine mission by a particular proof of his power over Satan; the conquest of Satan indicates the great design of his coming into the world, which was to destroy the works of the devil, and this cure is an earnest of that undertaking’s success. He notes with the others that Matthew describes the man as blind as well as dumb.

Robertson and Lightfoot handle the language of the charge. Robertson notes the construction of the opening clause, points out that the accusation is made here in Judea exactly as it had been in Galilee, and explains its logic: it was useless to deny the fact of the miracles, so they were attributed to Satan himself — an explanation he calls most absurd. On the demand for a sign he holds that these others had recognised the futility of the Beelzebub charge and shifted their ground, asking for a great spectacular display of heavenly power such as they expected from the Messiah and such as the devil had suggested on the pinnacle of the temple; the imperfect tense shows them keeping on at the demand. Lightfoot argues the form of the name, maintaining the reading Beelzebul with a final l against the Syriac, Persian, Vulgate and other versions that give Beelzebub, and noting that the Italian avoids the question with a form committing to neither.

Wesley makes two brief notes. On the first verse he observes that the spirit is called dumb because it made the man so. On the name he takes the other side of the textual question from Lightfoot and glosses it: Beelzebub signifies the lord of flies, a title the heathen gave to Jupiter, whom they accounted the chief of their gods and yet supposed to be employed in driving flies away from their temple and sacrifices; the Philistines worshipped a deity of that name as the god of Ekron, and from them the Jews took it.

Theophylact works on the word rendered dumb. It commonly means one who does not speak, but it is also used of one who does not hear, and most properly of one who neither hears nor speaks; and he draws the connection between the two disabilities, since a man who has not heard from his birth necessarily cannot speak, because what we speak is what we have been taught.
Cyril, whom the chain quotes immediately after Bede, records the crowd’s response rather than the exegesis: when the miracle had been performed the multitude extolled him with loud voice.

Gloss and Bede supply the connection and the figure. Gloss reads the miracle as evidence of the promise just made, that the Holy Spirit would be given to those who ask, its blessed effects being clearly shown in what immediately follows. Bede notes that Matthew reports the same demoniac as blind as well as dumb, so that three miracles were performed at one time on one man — the blind see, the dumb speaks, and the man possessed is set free — and takes the three as a pattern of what happens daily in the conversion of believers: the devil is first cast out, then they see the light, and then mouths that were before silent are loosed to speak the praises of God.

debates: How the name should be read. Lightfoot argues at length for Beelzebul with a final l, against the Syriac, Persian and Vulgate; Wesley works from Beelzebub and derives it as lord of flies, from the god of Ekron. Neither engages the other, but the chapter carries both readings side by side.

Why the accusation was made at all. Robertson holds that denial of the miracles was not open to the objectors, so attribution to Satan was the only course left, and calls it absurd; Gill locates the motive in their refusal to allow that Christ could be the Messiah.

What the demand for a sign was. Robertson takes it as a second line of attack after the first failed, asking for a Messianic spectacle; Calvin takes it as pretext-building, designed to justify unbelief by claiming the calling was unattested.
outliers: Bede alone turns the three simultaneous cures into a standing pattern of conversion — devil cast out, light seen, silent mouth opened — rather than treating them as three facts about one man.
Theophylact alone approaches the miracle through the physiology of the word, explaining why deafness from birth entails dumbness, where the rest are concerned with the charge that followed the cure.
themes: the miracle as a figure of conversion
the charge of casting out by Beelzebub
Christ’s power over Satan as proof of his mission

17.pericope_label: But he, knowing their thoughts, said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and a house divided against a house falleth. If Satan also be divided against himself, how shall his kingdom stand? because ye say that I cast out devils through Beelzebub. And if I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your sons cast them out? therefore shall they be your judges. But if I with the finger of God cast out devils, no doubt the kingdom of God is come upon you. When a strong man armed keepeth his palace, his goods are in peace: But when a stronger than he shall come upon him, and overcome him, he taketh from him all his armour wherein he trusted, and divideth his spoils. He that is not with me is against me: and he that gathereth not with me scattereth.

schools.summary: Gill works through the passage clause by clause. Christ knew their thoughts as God omniscient; the appeal to Satan divided against himself is the accommodation of the proverbs, showing that if the Pharisees were right Satan must be against himself and his government could not long subsist. He records that the Greek copies, with the Arabic and Ethiopic versions, spell the name with a final l, and that the Cabalistic Jews explain the finger of God as the power of God. The strong man he arms twice over: with his own temptations, fiery darts thrown thick and fast, suddenly and with great cunning, and with the sins and lusts of men, which are armour of unrighteousness that Satan turns back upon them; the stronger is Christ, the mighty God, shown so in creation, providence, redemption, conversion and preservation. On the last verse he guards against a misuse, denying that Christ means everyone not personally in his company, since many who were not with him in person were nevertheless friends to his interest.

Robertson and Ellicott handle grammar and idiom. Robertson notes that the word for their thoughts means intent or purpose and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; that both conditional sentences are of the first class, so that Jesus assumes the charge for the sake of argument, a Greek condition dealing only with the statement and not the facts; that the Jewish exorcists practised incantations against demons; that the verb in the conclusion about the kingdom means in late Greek simply to come rather than to come before, its tense here being timeless; and that in the parable the participle for fully armed is perfect and found only here, the palace is really a homestead, and the guarding is continuous where the assault is a single onset. Ellicott sets the finger of God in its Old Testament company: the older prophets’ ‘hand of the Lord’ for the state issuing in prophetic inspiration, the finger that wrote the commandments on the tables of stone, and the confession of Pharaoh’s magicians that the finger of God was with Moses and Aaron.

Wesley reads the two phrases for their force. The finger of God means a power manifestly divine, and he suggests the expression may intimate further that the work was done without any labour; the kingdom coming upon them he takes as coming unawares and unexpected, which he says the Greek word implies. On the parable he arms the strong man briefly and pointedly: the devil is strong in himself and armed with the pride, obstinacy and security of the man in whom he dwells.

Chrysostom, Theophylact and Basil supply successive links. Chrysostom explains why the charge had to be answered as a thought rather than a speech: the suspicion was utterly without reason, so the Pharisees dared not divulge it for fear of the multitude and only pondered it in their minds. On the strong man he refuses the obvious inference, holding that the devil is called strong not because he is naturally so but by reference to his ancient dominion, of which our own weakness was the cause; and he numbers the closing saying as the fourth answer in the series, arguing that one whose work is to scatter what belongs to Christ could not conceivably be united with him in casting out devils. Theophylact identifies the strong man’s arms as all kinds of sins, in which he trusted and by which he prevailed against men. Basil reads the division of the spoil as a picture of the watch that angels faithfully keep over the salvation of men.

Cyril twice supplies the turn of the argument. On the charge he reasons from its character: since what they say bears the mark of calumny, it is plain that the devils are cast out by the Spirit of God. On the parable he notes that many reasons made it necessary to refute the cavils, and that our Lord therefore uses a very plain example, which proves to anyone who will consider it that he overcomes the power of the world by a power inherent in himself.

Bede, Ambrose and Augustine take up the argument at three points. Bede observes that Christ answered their thoughts and not their words, so that they might be compelled to believe in the power of one who saw into the secrets of the heart; identifies ‘your sons’ as the Jewish exorcists who cast out devils by invoking God, and presses the parity — if their work is credited to God and not to devils, the same work should have the same cause in Christ; and explains that they will be judges in act rather than in authority. On the strong man he makes the palace the world, which lies in wickedness and in which the devil held supreme power until the Saviour’s coming, resting unopposed in the hearts of unbelievers, and reads the dividing of spoils as the sign of triumph, since leading captivity captive Christ gave gifts to men and ordained apostles, evangelists, prophets, pastors and teachers. Ambrose turns the maxim about divided kingdoms against the objectors: it shows Christ’s kingdom to be undivided and everlasting, while theirs is not, and he applies this to the Jewish people, asking how their kingdom can be everlasting when by the people of the law Jesus is denied whom the law promised. Augustine notes that Luke’s ‘finger of God’ where Matthew has ‘the Spirit’ does not disturb their agreement in sense but has something to teach.

debates: Why Luke writes ‘the finger of God’ where Matthew has ‘the Spirit of God’. Augustine denies any disagreement in sense and finds a lesson in the difference; Ellicott explains it from Old Testament idiom; Robertson takes it as marking the contrast with the Jewish exorcists; Gill reports the Cabalistic explanation as simply the power of God; Wesley adds that it may imply effortlessness.

What follows from the exorcists’ own practice. Bede and Robertson agree that the argument is conditional and turns on parity of cause, Bede adding that the sons will judge their fathers in act rather than in office.

In what sense the devil is strong. Chrysostom denies that the strength is natural and refers it to an ancient dominion permitted by human weakness; Gill and Wesley locate it in his armoury — temptations and the sins of men for Gill, the pride and security of his host for Wesley.

How far the closing saying reaches. Gill restricts it against a literal reading, since men not personally present with Christ were not thereby against him; Chrysostom applies it directly to the objectors, as men who scatter.
outliers: Basil alone reads the dividing of the spoil as angelic guardianship of human souls, where Bede in the same chain takes it as Christ’s triumphal distribution of ministerial gifts.
Ambrose alone extends the maxim about a divided kingdom into a national judgment, arguing that the Jewish polity cannot endure because it denies the Christ its own law promised.
themes: by whom do your sons cast them out
the kingdom of God come upon you
he that is not with me is against me

24.pericope_label: When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest; and finding none, he saith, I will return unto my house whence I came out. And when he cometh, he findeth it swept and garnished. Then goeth he, and taketh to him seven other spirits more wicked than himself; and they enter in, and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first.

schools.summary: Gill keeps the saying general and turns it against a merely outward profession. The unclean spirit is the devil who works in the children of disobedience, whether under a profession of religion or not, and delights to dwell where hearts are unclean like himself; he may be said to go out in appearance when a man outwardly reforms and takes up a profession. The swept and garnished house he holds to be empty of all goodness for all its sweeping, noting that Matthew and the Arabic version add ‘empty’ and the Ethiopic reads ‘empty of men’, while the Persic renders it ‘heated and prepared’ — heated with wrath and fury against Christ and his gospel, and so fitted to be a proper habitation for Satan. The seven spirits he takes to be brought in as consorts and companions.

Robertson restricts himself to the synoptic comparison. These verses are almost verbatim what stands in Matthew, and he lists the differences precisely: Luke has a present participle where Matthew has a present indicative for the finding of no rest; Matthew has the spirit take the others with himself where Luke has him simply take them; and Luke omits Matthew’s closing application to this evil generation. He notes the ablative after the comparative in the last clause, and remarks that the seven demons brought back recall the seven from which Mary Magdalene was delivered.

Wesley reaches the historical application by way of a historian rather than a typology. Anyone who reads the account Josephus gives of the temple and of the people’s conduct between the ascension of Christ and their final destruction by the Romans must acknowledge that no emblem could have been more proper: their characters were the vilest conceivable, and they pressed on to their own ruin as if possessed by legions of devils and wrought up to the last degree of madness. He then extends the saying beyond that generation, holding that it is fulfilled likewise in all who totally and finally fall away.

Chrysostom presses the national reading into contemporary history. The evil spirits now dwelling in those souls are worse than the earlier ones, since formerly the people raged against the prophets and now lift their hands against the Lord of the prophets; from which he concludes that they suffered worse things at the hands of Vespasian and Titus than they had suffered in Egypt or in Babylon. He adds that in the earlier case they still had the providence of God and the grace of the Holy Spirit with them, whereas now they are deprived even of that protection.

Cyril and Origen both read the parable of the returning spirit as an account of Israel. Cyril takes it as our Lord’s explanation of how the Jewish people arrived at their opinions concerning Christ, and grounds the identification on Matthew, who ends the same saying with the words about this wicked generation; he then supplies the history, that during their life in Egypt after the Egyptian manner an evil spirit dwelt in them and was drawn out when they sacrificed the lamb as a type of Christ. Origen glosses the house the spirit returns to as those of Israel in whom he saw nothing divine, but a place desolate and vacant for him to take up his abode there.

Ambrose and Bede divide over the reading. Ambrose develops the national interpretation most fully: the comparison is between one man and the whole Jewish people, from whom the unclean spirit had been cast out by the Law; among the Gentiles, whose hearts were barren at first but afterwards moistened in baptism with the dew of the Spirit, the devil could find no rest because of their faith, since to unclean spirits Christ is a flaming fire; and so he returned to the house he came from, Israel being adorned with a merely outward ornament. Bede declines the whole scheme and offers a plain alternative: the words may simply have been added to show the distinction between Satan’s work and Christ’s, the one ever hastening to cleanse what has been defiled and the other to defile with greater pollution what has been cleansed.

debates: Whether the passage is about the Jewish people or about any man. Cyril, Ambrose, Origen and Chrysostom all take it nationally, and Cyril grounds this on Matthew’s closing sentence about this wicked generation — the very sentence Robertson observes that Luke omits. Bede sets the national reading aside for a general contrast between Satan’s work and Christ’s, and Gill applies it to any outward reformation unaccompanied by goodness. Wesley takes both, applying it first to that generation and then to all who finally fall away.

What the emptiness of the house means. Gill argues it is empty of goodness rather than of occupants, against the versions that add ‘empty’ or ‘empty of men’, and notes a rendering that makes it heated and prepared for its returning tenant. Origen makes it the desolation of those with nothing divine in them; Ambrose calls it a merely outward ornament.

How far the worse last state was realised. Chrysostom names Vespasian and Titus and measures the suffering against Egypt and Babylon; Wesley appeals instead to Josephus on the state of the temple and the people before the Roman destruction.
outliers: Bede is the only witness here who refuses the historical application entirely, reducing the saying to a general statement about the opposed tendencies of Christ and Satan.

Robertson is alone in treating the passage purely as a text-critical comparison with Matthew, and his observation that Luke drops the application to this generation cuts against the reading the other witnesses build on it.
themes: the last state worse than the first

27.pericope_label: And it came to pass, as he spake these things, a certain woman of the company lifted up her voice, and said unto him, Blessed is the womb that bare thee, and the paps which thou hast sucked. But he said, Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin attend to the occasion and the intention. Gill places the exclamation exactly, as coming when Christ had finished the sayings by which he vindicated himself and his miracles from the blasphemy of the Scribes and Pharisees and had spoken the parable of the unclean spirit, which bore particularly on them; and on the reply he observes that Christ neither denied what the woman said nor reproved her for it, but corrected by improving upon it. Calvin insists that the woman’s aim was to magnify the excellence of Christ and that she can have had no reference to Mary, whom she had perhaps never seen; he adds that the blessing was nevertheless in strict accordance with the manner of scripture, which declares offspring — and particularly offspring endued with distinguished virtues — to be a remarkable gift of God.

Henry notes first that the passage stands in no other evangelist, and refuses to identify it with the earlier scene in which Christ’s mother and brethren desired to speak with him, which this same evangelist has already related; it is an interruption of the same kind, and like that one it becomes an occasion for instruction. He describes the speaker as an affectionate, honest, well-meaning woman, probably a person of some quality, and sets her admiration of the discourse directly against the scribes and Pharisees, who despised and blasphemed it.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the setting and the force of the answer. Barnes takes the woman to have supposed that the mother of such a person must be peculiarly happy, and reads the reply as an admission rather than a denial: Jesus grants that she was happy and that it was an honour to be his mother, while insisting that the chief happiness and highest honour lies in obeying the word of God, beside which all earthly distinctions and honours are nothing. Ellicott notes that the incident is peculiar to Luke and appears to have reached him from the company of devout women with whom he came into contact, and finds it interesting as the first direct fulfilment of the Magnificat’s ‘all generations shall call me blessed’, with Christ extending the beatitude as he does elsewhere; on the second verse he holds that ‘the word of God’ designates the message of the kingdom as our Lord spoke it, which in its wider application includes but must not be confined to the written record. Robertson observes Luke’s characteristic construction, calls this in a special sense the Gospel of Woman, quotes Bengel’s remark that she speaks well but womanly, connects her beatitude with Elisabeth’s greeting and with Mary’s own prophecy, and cites Plummer’s judgment that the originality of the reply guarantees its historical character, being beyond the reach of an inventor.

Clarke and Wesley both turn the reply into a test. Clarke thinks the exclamation very natural for a woman who was probably a mother herself, but holds that our Lord shows even the holy virgin could not be benefited merely by being mother of his human nature; they only are happy who carry Christ in their hearts, true happiness lying in hearing the glad tidings of salvation, keeping them in a holy heart and practising them. Wesley states the same in a single sentence: if even she who bore him had not heard the word of God and kept it, she would have forfeited all her blessedness.

Chrysostom takes the reply as neither disowning Mary nor conceding the woman’s premise. Christ did not seek to disown his mother, but to show that his birth would have profited her nothing had she not been really fruitful in works and in faith. From that he draws the argument a fortiori: if it profited Mary nothing that Christ derived his birth from her without the inward virtue of her heart, much less will it avail anyone to have a virtuous father, brother or son while he is himself a stranger to virtue.

Bede reads the interruption as a deliberate contrast placed where it stands. While the Scribes and Pharisees were tempting our Lord and uttering blasphemies against him, a woman with great boldness confessed his incarnation; and by that confession she refutes two things at once, the calumnies of the rulers then present and the unbelief of heretics still to come. The parallel he draws is exact: as the Jews of that moment denied the true Son of God by blaspheming the works of the Holy Spirit, so in later times heretics would deny the reality of his birth of the Virgin.

debates: What the woman meant by the blessing. Calvin holds she was magnifying Christ and had no reference to Mary at all, whom she had probably never seen; Barnes and Clarke read her as thinking directly of the mother’s happiness; Ellicott and Robertson hear in her words the fulfilment of Mary’s own prophecy that all generations would call her blessed.

Whether the reply corrects or merely extends her. Gill says Christ neither denied nor reproved but improved upon what she said; Barnes has him admit the honour while subordinating it; Chrysostom denies any disowning of his mother but makes the birth unprofitable without inward virtue; Wesley and Clarke press this hardest, holding that Mary herself would have forfeited her blessedness on those terms.

How wide ‘the word of God’ reaches. Ellicott identifies it primarily with the message of the kingdom as spoken by Christ, and warns against confining it to the written record while allowing that the record is included.
outliers: Bede alone reads the woman’s confession as an anticipatory refutation of later heresy about the incarnation, rather than as a spontaneous exclamation about motherhood.
Robertson alone treats the reply as evidence for the narrative’s authenticity, arguing from the originality of the saying that no inventor could have supplied it.
themes: blessed is the womb that bare thee
hearing and keeping the word of God
honour of natural relation to Christ
Luke as the Gospel of Woman
the word of God spoken and written

29.pericope_label: And when the people were gathered thick together, he began to say, This is an evil generation: they seek a sign; and there shall no sign be given it, but the sign of Jonas the prophet. For as Jonas was a sign unto the Ninevites, so shall also the Son of man be to this generation. The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with the men of this generation, and condemn them: for she came from the utmost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineve shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas is here.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin both explain what makes Jonah a sign. Gill describes it exactly — three days and three nights in the whale’s belly and then cast on shore alive — and gives its purpose, to confirm the prophet’s mission and message so that the Ninevites would credit him and repent. He also accounts for the crowd, gathering either at the woman’s outcry or rather to see what sign would be given; identifies the queen of the south as the queen of Sheba, a country of Arabia lying south of Judea; and observes that Luke reverses Matthew’s order of the two examples, putting Nineveh last, which he judges immaterial. Calvin fixes the sense of the word itself: it is not used here in its ordinary sense of pointing something out, but of what lies far outside the ordinary course of nature, Jonah’s mission being miraculous in that he was brought out of the fish’s belly as if from the grave to call men to repentance.

Henry reads the passage as answering what sign we may expect for the confirmation of our faith. His answer is the resurrection: the great and most convincing proof of Christ’s being sent of God, and the one they were still to wait for after many signs already given, was his rising from the dead. The demand itself he treats as deserving reproof, since the people were asking for other signs than those already given them in great plenty.

Clarke and Wesley both press the wording. Clarke would render the opening as ‘this is a wicked race of men’, and prefers an indefinite translation in the two examples — a queen of the south, and the men of this race, shall rise up in judgment — applying the same to the following verse. Wesley notes that the word for seeking implies seeking more, over and above what one already has, and carries the Nineveh comparison further than anyone else: the Ninevites repented only for a season and afterwards relapsed into wickedness until, some forty years later, they were destroyed; and the parallel holds, since these hearers were likewise reprieved for about forty years and still advanced in wickedness until, their measure being full, they were destroyed with an utter destruction.

Robertson and Lightfoot supply the philology and the rabbinic background. Robertson notes that the verb for the crowd’s gathering is rare, found only here in the New Testament, and means to throng together, giving a vivid picture of the press around Jesus; that Luke, unlike Matthew, does not here spell out the burial and resurrection which Jonah’s experience typified; that Luke has inserted the queen of the south between the two halves of the Jonah saying; that where Matthew writes simply ‘with this generation’ Luke writes ‘with the men of this generation’; and that both Solomon and Jonah stand in the ablative after the comparative. Lightfoot reports, with open puzzlement, the passage in Bava Bathra which holds that whoever says the queen of Sheba was a woman is simply mistaken and that what is meant is the kingdom of Sheba, and asks whether the whole kingdom of the Sabeans is then supposed to have come to Solomon.

Theophylact and Cyril of Jerusalem each use the Jonah sign for a particular end. Theophylact notes what followed the prophet’s deliverance, that after coming out of the whale’s belly he converted the men of the city. Cyril of Jerusalem employs the verse apologetically, against those who grant that a corpse lately dead was raised by the living but demand proof that a man three days dead can rise and that one buried can rise after three days; he answers that the Lord Jesus supplies the scriptural testimony himself in this saying about Jonah in the whale’s belly.

Bede, Ambrose, Augustine and Tertullian take four different approaches. Bede supplies the structure, noting that two kinds of question had been put — the charge about Beelzebub, answered up to this point, and the demand for a sign from heaven, which is answered from here. Ambrose reads the sign of Jonah as at once a type of our Lord’s passion and a testimony to grievous sin, and finds in it both a mighty voice of warning and a declaration of mercy: the Ninevites’ example denounces a punishment and promises a remedy, so that even these hearers need not despair of pardon if they will practise repentance. Augustine addresses the different order of the sayings in the two evangelists and refuses to treat it as a problem, holding it an idle question in what order our Lord spoke, since no one repeats another’s words in the order they were uttered and the order makes no difference to the fact. Tertullian is arguing rather than expounding: he is content to leave the faults the Marcionites find in the Creator to be refuted elsewhere, and presses instead that the same faults appear in the Christ they propose, who enjoins giving to everyone that seeks and then refuses to give a sign to those who seek one.

debates: What the sign of Jonah consists in. Calvin and Gill locate it in the deliverance from the fish, treated as a miracle attesting a mission; Ambrose makes it a type of the passion; Cyril of Jerusalem uses it as evidence specifically for a three-day resurrection. Robertson observes that Luke, unlike Matthew, leaves the burial and rising unstated here, so the identification is supplied from the parallel rather than from this text.

Whether the difference of order between the evangelists matters. Augustine calls the question idle and grounds his answer on how people actually report speech; Gill notes the same reversal in the two examples and judges it immaterial; Robertson describes the arrangement without comment.

Who the queen of the south was. Gill takes her straightforwardly as the queen of Sheba in Arabia; Lightfoot reports a rabbinic opinion that the phrase denotes the kingdom rather than a woman, and treats it as untenable; Clarke prefers to render the noun indefinitely in both examples.
outliers: Wesley alone extends the Nineveh comparison past the repentance to the relapse, making the city’s later destruction after forty years a parallel to the reprieve and ruin of the generation addressed.

Tertullian alone is using the refusal of a sign as a debating point against an opponent’s doctrine rather than as teaching, arguing that the Christ his adversaries propose is inconsistent for withholding what he elsewhere commands to be given.
themes: Jonah as a type of the passion
the resurrection as the promised sign
a greater than Solomon and Jonah
order and agreement of the evangelists

33.pericope_label: No man, when he hath lighted a candle, putteth it in a secret place, neither under a bushel, but on a candlestick, that they which come in may see the light. The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness. Take heed therefore that the light which is in thee be not darkness. If thy whole body therefore be full of light, having no part dark, the whole shall be full of light, as when the bright shining of a candle doth give thee light.

schools.summary: Gill treats both halves plainly. The saying about the candle is one Christ repeated on different occasions, and here it designs the free, open and clear ministry of Christ, who excelled Solomon in wisdom and Jonas in powerful preaching, and which is like a candle that no man lights in order to hide. On the eye he records that the Vulgate and all the eastern versions read ‘the light of thy body is thine eye’, and gives the sense: as the eye gives light to the body and its several members, so the understanding is the light of the soul and the guide of all its powers and faculties. The warning that follows he takes as a charge to attend to the light of the gospel in the ministration of it and not to neglect or despise it.

Clarke and Wesley both read the passage as being about intention. Clarke reverses the application of the lamp: to work a miracle among a people determined to disbelieve every evidence of his Messiahship would be to light a candle and then cover it with a bushel, preventing the very end for which it was lit. He records that the last two verses are wanting in some manuscripts and variously read in others, and explains the final one by the completeness of sight — when the eye is perfect, every object within its reach is as completely seen as if there were an eye in every part, and so the light of Christ dwelling fully in the heart reaches every thought, word and action. Wesley makes the single eye a question of aim: God gives this gospel light that men may repent, and one who fixes his eye singly on God and aims only at pleasing him will be full of wisdom, holiness and happiness, while one who aims at anything else will be full of folly, sin and misery.

Lightfoot, Ellicott and Robertson supply connection, comparison and grammar. Lightfoot grants that the coherence of this passage with what precedes is a little difficult, and proposes that since two objections had been raised — the charge about the prince of the devils and the demand for a sign — this passage answers both, but the second more principally; on the last verse, which he finds nearly tautologous, he explains that our Saviour speaks of the eye after the manner of the schools, where the evil eye, or the eye not single, denoted the covetous, envious and malicious mind. Ellicott judges the sequence of thought in Luke different from Matthew’s and in some respects closer, noting that in the Sermon on the Mount the disciples are themselves the light and the teaching about the light of the body is separated from that illustration by the comment on scribal tradition; on the warning he prefers ‘see to it whether the light that is in thee be darkness’, standing where Matthew has the exclamation about the greatness of that darkness, and reads it as a call to examine one’s primary beliefs and very intuitions of right and wrong, lest everything one does be vitiated at its source. Robertson notes that the word for the secret place means a crypt, is late and rare and occurs only here in the New Testament, that the construction of the indirect question is good Greek, and that it is a pitiful situation when the very light is darkness, as happens when the eye of the soul is too diseased to see the light of Christ.

Theophylact and Chrysostom take the analogy at its plainest and press its consequence. Theophylact sets the two terms side by side: as the body is light when the bodily eye is light and dark when the eye is dark, so it is with the understanding in relation to the soul. Chrysostom follows in the same chain with the case that follows from it, asking what becomes of a man when the very faculty capable of admitting light has itself been corrupted.

Cyril and Origen contribute the occasion and the psychology. Cyril supplies the calumny the saying answers: the Jews maintained that Christ performed his miracles not for faith, that men might believe in him, but to gain the applause of the spectators and so acquire more followers; the image of the lamp openly set refutes that account of his motive. Origen takes the singleness of the eye as native to the mind itself, which from its very beginning desires only singleness, containing in itself no dissimulation, no guile and no division.

Bede and Gregory read the figure very differently. Bede takes the lighted candle for Christ himself, and finds in it a qualification of what has just been said: though no sign was to be given this generation but the sign of Jonas, his own brightness was not a thing to be hidden away. Gregory declines the usual identification of the body with the whole person and makes it each particular action, which follows its own intention as an action follows the eye of those who watch it; the light of the body is the eye because it is by the ray of a good intention that the deserving parts of a work receive their light, so that where we intend rightly in singleness of heart we accomplish a good work even when it does not appear to be good.

debates: How this saying connects with what precedes it. Lightfoot concedes the difficulty and refers the passage to both earlier objections, chiefly the demand for a sign; Cyril refers it to the charge that the miracles were done for applause; Bede reads it as Christ qualifying his own refusal of a sign; Clarke reverses the figure so that withholding a miracle from an obstinate people is itself the hiding of the candle.

What the body stands for. Theophylact and Gill take it as the soul under the guidance of the understanding; Gregory takes it as each individual action considered under its intention, which yields a different conclusion — that a rightly intended work is good even when it does not look so.

What the eye being evil means. Lightfoot derives it from the language of the schools, where it denoted a covetous, envious and malicious mind; Wesley makes it a matter of aiming at anything other than God; Origen and Chrysostom treat it as the corruption of a faculty naturally single.
outliers: Gregory alone shifts the whole figure from the person to the single act, so that the saying becomes a rule about intention in particular works rather than about the state of the soul.
Clarke alone reports that verses 35 and 36 are absent from some manuscripts and read variously in others, a textual point none of the other witnesses on this passage raises.
themes: the lighted candle and the bushel
the ministry of Christ made public
the eye as lamp of the body
intention and the goodness of an action
comparison with the Sermon on the Mount

37.pericope_label: And as he spake, a certain Pharisee besought him to dine with him: and he went in, and sat down to meat. And when the Pharisee saw it, he marvelled that he had not first washed before dinner. And the Lord said unto him, Now do ye Pharisees make clean the outside of the cup and the platter; but your inward part is full of ravening and wickedness. Ye fools, did not he that made that which is without make that which is within also? But rather give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin work on the wording and on the nature of the reproof. Gill notes what the Pharisee actually saw, that Christ laid himself down on the couch and began to eat, and finds the phrase rendered ‘such things as ye have’ variously given — the Syriac ‘give that which is’, the Persic ‘which is given to you’, the Vulgate differently again — observing that the common English sense is an odd one, since nobody can give of what he has not. Calvin distinguishes this passage from the parallel in Matthew and Mark: Christ does not here charge the Pharisees with serving God by human inventions and breaking his law for their traditions, but merely glances at their hypocrisy in desiring purity only before the eyes of men, as if they had not to deal with God, and the reproof therefore reaches all hypocrites. On the alms he holds that Christ withdraws them from ceremonies to charity, declaring that it is not water but liberality — an active disposition to do good to those in want — which cleanses both men and food, without thereby disparaging the grace of God or rejecting the ceremonies of the Law as vain.

Henry frames the episode by its relation to the public discourse in the temple. Christ says here at a Pharisee’s table, in private conversation with the host and his guests, many of the things he afterwards said openly against the scribes and Pharisees; and Henry makes the coincidence a point of character, since what Christ said in public and in private was of a piece, and he would not say in a corner what he durst not repeat and stand to in the great congregation.

Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot supply the customs, the grammar and the rabbinic background. Barnes suggests the host invited Christ because he had felt the force of the preceding rebukes and wished to be alone with him, explains his astonishment by the mixed multitude whose touch was held polluting, glosses ‘ravening’ as robbery and plunder so that the vessels were filled with what had been unjustly taken, and notes that this terrible charge was pressed on the very man who had issued the invitation. On the alms he takes the property to be theirs though unjustly gained, and giving it to the poor the way to show repentance. Ellicott explains that the word for dining means a morning or noon-tide meal as distinct from the evening supper, holds that the washing implies immersion or at least a process taking in the whole body, and observes that this section stands to the great discourse against the Pharisees as the Sermon on the Plain stands to the Sermon on the Mount — not a narrative misplaced but words actually repeated; the last two verses he marks as peculiar to Luke, the question about the Maker implying a latent parable in which ceremonial and moral law have the same Author and neither is to be neglected for the other. Robertson insists the construction means ‘in the speaking’ and not ‘after he had spoken’, notes the dramatic present of the request, takes the verb for washing as dipping applied to the hands according to the custom of dipping before eating and between courses, distinguishes the platter from Matthew’s side-dish, and admits candidly that the phrase for what is within occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and that its meaning is not clear. Lightfoot doubts the whole-body washing, since there was neither need nor custom to wash more than the hands before meat; argues from ‘your inward parts’ that the rebuke concerns persons and not vessels; documents ‘fools’ as a word very common in the nation with rabbinic instances; and suspects the sentence about alms is spoken ironically, in derision of the opinion they held concerning almsgiving.

Clarke and Wesley keep close to the practical sense. Clarke explains the meal from the Jewish day, which had two meals only, so that this one served as both breakfast and dinner and was slight, the chief meal being supper after the heat of the day, as also among Greeks and Romans. On the question about the Maker he argues from the vessel’s purpose: its maker formed it outwardly and inwardly to answer an end it cannot answer unless clean within as well as without. On the alms he takes the phrase to mean what was in the dishes, or in their houses and power, or whatever was at hand, and turns the command into its opposite practice — cease from rapine, and instead of spoiling the poor by wicked exactions give them alms of everything you possess. Wesley notes that many Pharisees were probably present at the house, and reads the command as a demonstration: by acts directly contrary to rapine and wickedness they were to show that their hearts were cleansed, which would make the outward washings needless.

Chrysostom takes the command about alms at face value and commends it above the other discipline. He notes first that what is enjoined is almsgiving and not injury, almsgiving being precisely what is free from all injury; it makes all things clean and is more excellent than fasting, for though fasting is the more painful, almsgiving is the more profitable. It enlightens the soul, enriches it and makes it good and beautiful; and one who resolves to have compassion on the needy will the sooner cease from sin.
Cyril supplies the setting: while our Lord still continued speaking, the Pharisee invited him to his own house, and he went in and reclined at the meal.

Bede, Augustine, Ambrose and Cyprian each take one part. Bede presses Luke’s wording, that the words ‘he spoke these things’ show our Lord had not finished what he purposed to say but was interrupted by the invitation; on the alms he supplies a limit, since what is commanded is what is over and above our necessary food and clothing, no one being commended for giving so as to consume himself by want. Augustine describes the practice at issue — the Pharisees washed themselves with water every day before dinner, as if a daily washing could be a cleansing of the heart — and observes that the host uttered not a word but thought within himself, and was answered by one who perceives the secrets of the heart. Ambrose reads the vessel as the body, an earthly and fragile thing that breaks when let fall even a short distance, and notes that what the mind meditates within it readily expresses through the senses and actions of the body, just as what a cup holds within makes a glitter outside. Cyprian draws the pastoral consequence of the command to give alms: the Merciful bids us show mercy, and because he seeks to save those he redeemed at a great price, he teaches that those defiled after the grace of baptism may be made clean again.

debates: How much of the body the Pharisaic washing covered. Ellicott holds the word implies immersion or a process taking in the whole body; Lightfoot calls that hardly credible, since neither need nor custom required more than the hands; Robertson takes the verb as dipping and applies it to the hands.

Whether the rebuke concerns vessels or persons. Lightfoot settles it from the phrase ‘your inward parts’, which cannot be said of a cup; Ambrose reads the cup as the body; Barnes takes the vessels literally as filled with the proceeds of extortion.

What ‘give alms of such things as ye have’ means. Chrysostom, Calvin and Cyprian take the command straight, as charity replacing ceremony; Bede limits it to what is over and above necessities; Barnes applies it to unjustly gained property as an act of repentance; Clarke reads it as a call to cease from rapine; Gill finds the received rendering odd, since none can give what he has not; Robertson admits the phrase is unparalleled and obscure; and Lightfoot suspects the whole sentence is ironical.

How this passage relates to the discourse in Matthew. Ellicott treats it as words genuinely repeated rather than a misplaced narrative; Henry makes the repetition a point about Christ’s consistency in public and private; Calvin distinguishes the charge here from the sharper one recorded elsewhere.
outliers: Lightfoot alone hears irony in the command about alms, which every other witness reads as a straightforward instruction — a reading that would reverse the sense of the verse.
Barnes alone confronts the awkwardness of telling men to give away what they gained by extortion, and answers it by treating the gift as evidence of repentance rather than as restitution.
themes: the outside of the cup and platter
he that made the outside made the inside
give alms of such things as ye have
hypocrisy before the eyes of men

42.pericope_label: But woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye tithe mint and rue and all manner of herbs, and pass over judgment and the love of God: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. Woe unto you, Pharisees! for ye love the uppermost seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the markets. Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are as graves which appear not, and the men that walk over them are not aware of them.

schools.summary: Gill settles the relation to Matthew at the outset: though these woes and several other passages of this chapter are much alike with those in Matthew, it is clear that they were spoken at different times, these in the house of a Pharisee and those in the temple at Jerusalem. On the second woe he adds the uppermost rooms at feasts to the uppermost seats in the synagogues. On the third he takes up the address itself, noting that ‘Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites’ is what Matthew uses all along but occurs in Luke only here, that the Vulgate reduces the clause to a bare ‘woe unto you’ and drops the rest, and that the full form is retained in all the Oriental versions.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the detail. Barnes describes rue as a small garden plant used as a medicine, with a rosy flower, a bitter penetrating taste and a strong smell. Ellicott collects the verbal differences from Matthew — rue and all manner of herbs against anise and cummin, judgment and the love of God against the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy and faith — and judges them sufficient to show that the two accounts are independent; on the last woe he observes that the comparison, though drawn from the same object as Matthew’s, presents a different phase of it, since in Matthew the contrast lies between the whitened surface and the decaying bones within, whereas here the whitewash has worn away and nothing distinguishes the graves at all, and he notes that the better manuscripts give simply ‘Woe unto you, Pharisees’. Robertson works through the same variations grammatically: the verb for tithing is a late form meaning to take a tenth off; rue is a botanical term of later writers named from its thick leaves; the expression for every herb is a general one where Matthew has cummin; the verb for passing over means to go by or beside, where Matthew says they left the matter undone; and the chief seat stands in the singular here against Matthew’s plural, the seat itself being a semi-circular bench that faced the congregation.

Clarke and Wesley both keep to short, practical notes. Wesley defines the refrain, that the woe means ‘miserable are you’, and directs that the phrase be understood so throughout the chapter.
