Clarke observes on the second woe that every one of the Pharisees affected to be a ruler in the synagogues, and on the third draws out the difference from Matthew at length: there they are told they resemble whitewashed tombs, which have no fairness but on the outside, while here they are like hidden tombs, graves distinguished by no outward decoration and not raised above the ground, so that those who walked over them did not consider what corruption lay within — and just so, under the veil of hypocrisy, they covered their iniquities from those who had any dealings with them.

debates: Whether these woes are the same discourse as Matthew 23. Gill argues from the setting that they were spoken on a different occasion, in a private house rather than the temple; Ellicott and Robertson argue the same independence from the wording, listing substitutions in the list of herbs and in the weightier matters passed over.

What the figure of the graves means. Clarke and Ellicott agree that Luke’s image is not Matthew’s: Matthew contrasts a whitened exterior with the corruption inside, while Luke’s graves are unmarked altogether, the danger lying in their being unrecognised rather than in their being disguised.

Whether the third woe names the scribes. Ellicott reports that the better manuscripts read simply ‘Woe unto you, Pharisees’; Gill notes that the longer address is Matthew’s usual form, that Luke has it only here, and that the Vulgate cuts the clause back to the bare woe while the Oriental versions keep it whole.
outliers: Barnes alone leaves the argument to describe the plant, giving the flower, taste and smell of rue rather than the force of the reproach.
Wesley alone stops to define the recurring word, glossing the woe as a statement of misery rather than a curse, and extends that reading across the whole chapter.
themes: judgment and the love of God
these ought ye to have done
the uppermost seats in the synagogues

45.pericope_label: Then answered one of the lawyers, and said unto him, Master, thus saying thou reproachest us also. And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers. Woe unto you! for ye build the sepulchres of the prophets, and your fathers killed them. Truly ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres. Therefore also said the wisdom of God, I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they shall slay and persecute: That the blood of all the prophets, which was shed from the foundation of the world, may be required of this generation; From the blood of Abel unto the blood of Zacharias, which perished between the altar and the temple: verily I say unto you, It shall be required of this generation. Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.

schools.summary: Gill treats the parties and two phrases. He holds that the Scribes and lawyers were the same sort of persons, interpreters of the law and as tenacious of the traditions of the elders as the Pharisees, generally Pharisees themselves though some may have been of the sect of the Sadducees. On the wisdom of God he notes that the Syriac reads simply ‘wisdom’, and that it is usual with the Jews to represent the divine perfections as speaking, as they do with justice and mercy. On the blood he explains why Abel heads the list: he is named because he was the first man slain, and because he was slain on account of his righteousness, some copies and versions reading ‘righteous Abel’ or ‘innocent Abel’.

Lightfoot, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson divide the technical work. Lightfoot notes the small difficulty that the preceding woe addressed scribes and Pharisees while the answer comes from a lawyer, and suspects the Vulgate omitted the words on that account; he identifies the lawyers as the doctors of traditions, confirmed by the fact that everything reproached here is traditional; and he compares the phrase about the wisdom of God with the common rabbinic form in which the rule of judgment is made to speak. Barnes concedes it is not known how the lawyers differed from the scribes or to which party they belonged, reads the protest as the man’s conscience applying the discourse to himself, and takes the wisdom of God for the Saviour himself, since what follows stands nowhere in the Old Testament. Ellicott finds in the protest a sense at once of distinctness and of class fellowship, prefers the reading ‘truly are ye witnesses, and ye allow’, insists that ‘allow’ means approving of and having pleasure in, and notes the variation from Matthew’s ‘all the righteous blood’. Robertson glosses the verb of the protest as denoting outrageous treatment and positive insult, observes that the word for ‘grievous to be borne’ is late and stands here alone in the critical text, calls the argument about the tombs subtle but just — the building looks like disapproval while the reality is neglect and opposition — and doubts that Jesus is here describing himself as the wisdom of God, preferring that God in his wisdom said it.

Clarke and Wesley keep the application direct. Clarke observes that only he who searches the heart could unmask such hypocrites, and did it so effectually that their own consciences echoed the reproach; that the burdens were the traditions of the elders, to which the lawyers themselves paid little attention; that in acknowledging their fathers killed the prophets they are about to show, by their conduct toward Christ and his apostles, that they have not degenerated; that the words about the wisdom of God seem to be Luke’s own; and that the particle in the clause about the blood should be rendered ‘so that’, marking the event and not the design. Wesley identifies the lawyers as scribes and expounders of the law, reads the building of sepulchres as pretended reverence for ancient prophets by men destroying the prophets sent to themselves, finds the substance of the wisdom of God’s saying in many places of scripture though not in these words, and takes the requiring of the blood to mean that it shall be visibly and terribly punished.

Theophylact, Gregory of Nyssa and the Greek Exposition supply distinction, application and legend. Theophylact separates the two groups: the Pharisees, being separated from the rest, had the appearance of a religious sect, while those skilled in the Law were the Scribes and Doctors who solved legal questions. Gregory of Nyssa turns the woe about burdens into a description of a permanent type — many severe judges of sinners who are weak combatants, burdensome imposers of laws who are weak bearers of burdens, unwilling to approach or touch strictness of life though they exact it sternly from their subjects. The Greek Exposition records an alternative account of the death of Zacharias: at the murder of the children, John was to have been slain with the rest of his age, but Elizabeth snatched him from the slaughter and fled to the desert, and Herod’s soldiers, unable to find mother or child, turned their wrath on Zacharias and killed him as he ministered in the temple.

Cyril and Athan — so the chain abbreviates the name — each contribute one observation. Cyril accounts for the interruption psychologically — a reproof which exalts the meek is generally hateful to the proud man, so that the whole body of lawyers was struck with consternation when the Pharisees were blamed — and holds that Christ then brings a severe charge against them and subdues their foolish pride by an obvious example, the Law itself having been burdensome. Athan takes up the requiring of the prophets’ blood and argues from the behaviour of persecutors: if they kill, the death of the slain cries out the louder against them, and if they pursue, the flight of the sufferers is itself a memorial of the pursuers’ iniquity, since no one flees from the merciful and gentle but from the cruel and evil-minded.

Bede, Ambrose and Augustine handle conscience, imitation and the key. Bede observes how grievous a state that conscience is in which, on hearing the word of God, takes it for a reproach against itself; and he explains the untouched burdens as the Law which the lawyers pretend to keep and hand on to others while fulfilling it at no point themselves. Ambrose calls the saying about the sepulchres a good answer to a foolish superstition: those who build the prophets’ tombs condemn their fathers’ deeds, and then by rivalling their fathers’ wickedness throw the sentence back upon themselves, since it is not the building but the imitation of the deeds that is reckoned a crime. He extends the last woe beyond its first hearers to all who usurp to themselves the teaching of divine knowledge, hinder others, and do not acknowledge what they profess; and he notes that Matthew records all this as spoken after our Lord had come into Jerusalem, whereas Luke relates it here. Augustine identifies the key of knowledge with the humility of Christ, which they would neither understand themselves nor allow to be understood by others.

debates: Whether the lawyers were a distinct body from the scribes. Theophylact separates them, making the Pharisees a sect in appearance and the lawyers the doctors who resolved legal questions; Gill treats scribes and lawyers as the same sort of men; Wesley identifies them outright; Barnes admits the difference is simply not known; Ellicott finds the speaker conscious of being something more than a scribe yet bound to their fate.

What the burdens are. Bede takes them for the Law itself, which the lawyers transmit without keeping; Lightfoot and Clarke restrict them to traditions, Lightfoot arguing that everything reproached in the passage is traditional.

Who is meant by ‘the wisdom of God’. Barnes says undoubtedly the Saviour himself, since the quotation is nowhere in the Old Testament; Clarke takes the phrase for Luke’s own comment; Robertson doubts Jesus would so describe himself and prefers that God in his wisdom spoke; Wesley finds the substance scattered through scripture; Lightfoot and Gill compare the Jewish idiom of making a divine attribute speak.
How Zacharias died. The Greek Exposition preserves a tradition that he was killed by Herod’s soldiers for hiding the infant John, which none of the other witnesses here reports.
Whether the clause about the blood states a purpose or a result. Clarke argues the particle should be rendered ‘so that’, marking only the event; Robertson calls it a divinely ordered sequence.
outliers: Gregory of Nyssa alone converts the woe into a description of a recurring class of religious authority rather than an accusation against these hearers, applying it to severe judges of sinners in his own day.
Athan alone argues from the psychology of persecution, treating flight from a persecutor as itself evidence against him, where the others treat the prophets’ blood as a matter of accumulated guilt.
themes: the blood of all the prophets

53.pericope_label: And as he said these things unto them, the scribes and the Pharisees began to urge him vehemently, and to provoke him to speak of many things: Laying wait for him, and seeking to catch something out of his mouth, that they might accuse him.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take opposite scales. Gill keeps to the immediate connection, that this followed Christ’s denouncing the woes upon them, charging them with those crimes and threatening them with divine vengeance, and glosses the last verse as watching his words in order to ensnare and entangle him. Calvin raises the question of the whole chapter’s arrangement, holding that the preceding sentences were not inserted by Luke in their proper place: while relating that Christ reproved the scribes at a dinner, the evangelist has introduced also the latest discourses, by which a little before his death Christ reproved their wicked courses. He does not press the point, adding that he has no great objection if anyone prefers to think Christ repeated the same discourses on different occasions.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the setting and the vocabulary. Barnes describes the tactic exactly: they pressed upon him violently, putting many questions about many matters without giving proper time to answer, asking as fast and as widely as possible so that in the hurry he might say something wrong, which he calls a remarkable instance of their cunning, malignity and unfairness; the last clause he takes as laying snares rather than lying in wait, on the analogy of men who catch birds by deceiving them and taking them unawares, with a view to accusing him before the great council and so securing his death. He ends with a general lesson, that faithful reproofs must be expected to excite opposition and hatred, since rousing a man’s conscience does not prevent his hating the reproof and the reprover. Ellicott reports that the better manuscripts begin the sentence with words meaning that Jesus had gone forth from thence, so that he had left the house after the last woe and was followed by the crowd of angry disputants; that the verb rendered ‘provoke to speak’ means literally to cause a man to speak impromptu and without thought; and that the better text gives the last clause in a simpler form, whose wording throws light on the later question about tribute to Caesar and shows it to have been the acting out of a pre-concerted policy. Robertson takes the same view of the departure, notes that we are not told what became of the breakfast but that the rage of Pharisees and lawyers knew no bounds, explains the verb for pressing upon him as meaning to hold in, to be enraged at, to have it in for someone — the same word used of Herodias’s relentless hatred of John the Baptist — traces the verb for provoking to a root meaning the mouth, used by Plato of making a pupil recite from memory, and finds in the two words of the last verse a picture drawn from ambush and from the chase, as of rabbis treating Jesus like a beast of prey.

Clarke renders the first verb as beginning to be furious, and explains the fury by their situation: they found themselves completely unmasked in the presence of a vast concourse of people. He denies that all this conversation can have passed while Christ was still at meat in the Pharisee’s house, since the parallel in Matthew shows the words were spoken on another occasion; and he describes the purpose of the questioning, that by the multitude and the impertinence of their questions they hoped to puzzle or irritate him into speaking rashly, so that they might find something against him.

debates: Where the scene takes place. Ellicott and Robertson follow the better manuscripts in reading that Jesus had gone out of the house, so that the questioning happens outside; Clarke reaches a similar conclusion from the parallel in Matthew rather than from the text; Gill leaves the connection where the received text puts it.

Whether Luke has kept the original order. Calvin holds he has not, and that discourses from shortly before the passion have been gathered into the dinner scene, while allowing the alternative that Christ repeated himself on different occasions; Clarke argues the same conclusion from Matthew’s placing of the words.

What the questioning was for. Barnes and Clarke agree that speed and volume were the method, meant to produce a rash word rather than an answer; Ellicott finds the same in the verb itself, which denotes speaking impromptu and unconsidered; Robertson adds that the vocabulary of the last verse comes from ambush and hunting.
outliers: Ellicott alone looks forward out of the chapter, treating this closing verse as evidence that the later attempt to trap Christ over the tribute money was part of a policy settled here rather than an improvised question.
Barnes alone turns the passage into a general rule about the reception of reproof, observing that a roused conscience does not soften the hearer toward the one who roused it.
themes: provoking him to speak unconsidered words
questions asked without time to answer
language of ambush and the chase
intent to accuse before the council
